sections.title: The Fifth Vision: Judgment at the Altar

blocks.text: The vision shows the Lord standing beside the altar, commanding the sanctuary's destruction. The capitals of the building are to be shattered, causing the thresholds to shake, with catastrophic collapse of the structure and those within it. While certain textual details present interpretive challenges, the core image is unambiguous: the sanctuary itself becomes a place of judgment rather than refuge.

The vision then pursues the theme of inescapable judgment through an escalating series of locations. Whether people descend to Sheol, ascend to heaven, hide atop Mount Carmel, or plunge into the sea, God's hand seizes them. Even exile before enemies cannot prevent the sword from reaching them. This relentless cataloging emphasizes the absoluteness of divine judgment and the futility of resistance or hiding.

The early Christian community interpreted this restoration promise expansively. Acts 15:16-18 quotes a Greek form of Amos 9:11-12 in the context of including gentiles in God's people, associating the restored Davidic tent with the remnant of humanity and nations called by God's name. This reuse demonstrates how interpreters beyond the original context understood the restoration as extending beyond Israel to encompass gentile nations.

The Masoretic and Old Greek textual traditions of Amos represent related but sometimes divergent forms. Early Hebrew manuscripts including 4Q78, 4Q82, 5QAmos, and MurXII preserve the textual history of the book in antiquity, attesting to how Amos circulated and was read in early Jewish communities.
